title: Woodridge Apartment Fire Displaces 57, Damages 41 Units
description: A gas-fed fire at Windsor Lakes Apartment Homes in Woodridge, Illinois, burned for more than nine hours, damaging 41 units and displacing 57 residents.
key_points: A fire at Windsor Lakes Apartment Homes in Woodridge on Sept. 24 damaged 41 units across three buildings and displaced 57 residents.
Three residents and one firefighter were hospitalized in stable condition, and officials said natural gas fed the fire, though the cause remains undetermined.
All displaced residents found temporary housing, and the village has listed donation sites for food, gift cards, clothing and personal care items.
body_html:
A daylong fire at a suburban Chicago apartment complex has left 57 people without homes after flames, fed in part by natural gas, spread through three buildings at Windsor Lakes Apartment Homes in Woodridge, Illinois. Village officials said 41 apartment units were damaged in the Thursday, Sept. 24, blaze, which took firefighters more than nine hours to fully extinguish.

What happened

The Darien-Woodridge Fire Protection District was called to a structure fire on the 7300 block of Woodward Avenue at about 10 a.m., according to a Village of Woodridge press release. Crews reported flames visible from the building when they arrived, and ABC7 Chicago reported that part of the roof collapsed during the fight. At least five neighboring agencies assisted, and Woodward Avenue was closed near 75th Street while crews worked.

The fire was not fully out until roughly 7:30 p.m. Officials said the presence of natural gas complicated suppression efforts. Utility crews from Nicor Gas and ComEd shut off gas and power to the affected area, according to CBS Chicago.

Who was affected

The village reported that 41 units were affected and 57 residents displaced. Three residents and one firefighter were taken to a hospital; officials described all four as stable. No deaths were reported. Fire Chief Jimmy Lahanis credited firefighters, police and supporting agencies with working together to evacuate residents safely.

By the following morning, all of the displaced residents had found temporary housing, according to Shaw Local.

Response and aid

The American Red Cross set up a temporary shelter offering meals, counseling, spiritual care and a place to sleep, and the village said it was coordinating assistance alongside the agency. Residents seeking help were directed to the Red Cross line at 1-800-733-2767.

Several days after the fire, the community organized donation channels, Shaw Local reported:

  • Gift cards and food at the West Suburban Community Pantry, 6809 Hobson Valley Drive, Suite 118.
  • Blankets, clothing and personal care items at the Windsor Lakes leasing office, 7499 Woodward Avenue.
  • Monetary donations through the nonprofit Woodridge Neighbors Helping Neighbors.

Mayor Gina Cunningham said the community's strength is often most visible in its hardest moments.

Cause and investigation

The cause has not been determined. Lahanis told CBS Chicago that natural gas "did play into this fire," but said the actual cause was undetermined while investigators completed their work. The origin and cause investigation remains open.

What this means for renters

Fires that involve natural gas or roof collapses can keep buildings closed for long stretches, because utilities and structural engineers both have to sign off before anyone moves back in. For displaced tenants, the first weeks matter most:

  • Get your status in writing. Ask management whether your unit is considered uninhabitable and what that means for rent due during the closure. Most leases address what happens when a unit is destroyed or made unlivable, so read your lease's casualty or fire clause.
  • Call your renters insurer right away. Many policies include "additional living expenses" or "loss of use" coverage that pays for hotels and meals while you are displaced. Keep every receipt.
  • Document what you can. Photos, bank and card statements, and online order histories help rebuild an inventory of lost belongings for a claim.
  • Know the smell of gas. If you ever smell rotten eggs in your building, leave first and call 911 or your gas utility from outside. Do not flip switches or use lighters on the way out.

If you are among the displaced, keep in contact with the Red Cross and the village, which said it would share updates through its website, social media and E-News.

title: Somerville Five-Alarm Fire Displaces 43 in Teele Square
description: A five-alarm fire tore through a mixed-use building in Somerville's Teele Square on Sept. 30, displacing 43 residents from 32 homes. A relief fund is open.
key_points: A five-alarm fire on Sept. 30 at 1137-1147 Broadway in Somerville displaced 43 residents from 32 homes above ground-floor businesses.
All residents escaped without injury; two firefighters were treated at a hospital for minor injuries, and the cause is under investigation.
Somerville and the Somerville Homeless Coalition activated the Emergency Displacement Fund to give displaced residents direct financial help.
body_html:
Forty-three people lost their homes on Wednesday, Sept. 30, when a five-alarm fire swept through the upper floors of a three-story mixed-use building in Somerville's Teele Square, city officials said. Everyone inside got out safely, but the fire and the water used to fight it left the building's 32 apartments unlivable.

Timeline

The fire broke out at about 4:50 p.m. in the building at 1137-1147 Broadway, near Curtis Street, according to Patch. Flames moved through the third floor and roof, and the response escalated to five alarms. Firefighters from Arlington, Boston, Brookline, Belmont, Cambridge, Chelsea, Everett, Malden, Medford, Revere and Watertown assisted the Somerville Fire Department, and Medford supplied a drone to help commanders track the fire. Crews had the blaze under control by about 6 p.m.

Somerville Fire Chief Charles Breen told The Boston Globe that the fire required "a lot of manpower." He said all occupants were out, and firefighters also rescued two cats.

Who was affected

The city said the fire affected 32 homes and displaced 43 residents. No residents were hurt. Two firefighters were taken to a hospital for minor injuries.

The third floor and roof took heavy fire and smoke damage, while lower floors suffered extensive water damage, Patch reported. The building's ground floor houses several businesses, including Teele Square Coin Laundry, Happy Crab, Masala and Bluemoon Smoke and Vape Outlets, all of which were affected.

Mayor Jake Wilson said first responders "worked tirelessly" and that, thankfully, no residents were injured.

Aid for displaced residents

City staff and the American Red Cross are coordinating temporary housing and immediate needs, the City of Somerville said. The city and the Somerville Homeless Coalition also activated the Emergency Displacement Fund, which provides direct financial assistance to Somerville residents displaced by fires and other emergencies. The city is directing donors to bit.ly/shcfund and says gifts of any size help. The Board of Health was working to identify all affected households, according to the Globe.

Residents who need language assistance or accessibility support can contact the city's ADA coordinator at 617-625-6600, ext. 2059, or email languageaccess@somervillema.gov.

Cause

The cause of the fire is under investigation. Officials have not released any preliminary findings.

What renters in older mixed-use buildings should know

Apartments above storefronts are common in Greater Boston and in older neighborhoods nationwide. These buildings can carry extra risk because commercial kitchens, laundries and retail spaces sit directly beneath homes, and fires that reach roofs and attics can spread quickly. This fire also shows how water damage can displace tenants on floors the flames never touched.

  • Know two ways out. In walk-up buildings, identify your main stairway and a second exit, such as a rear stair or fire escape, and keep both clear.
  • Test smoke alarms monthly. Massachusetts requires working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in rental units. If yours is missing or not working, report it to your landlord in writing and, if it is not fixed, to your local board of health or fire department.
  • Insure your belongings. A landlord's policy covers the building, not your furniture, clothes or electronics. Renters insurance usually costs a modest monthly amount and can also cover temporary housing.
  • If displaced, ask about your lease. Ask your landlord in writing how rent will be handled while your unit is uninhabitable, and contact local legal aid if you are unsure of your rights under Massachusetts law.

Displaced Somerville residents should stay in contact with the Red Cross and city staff about housing and fund eligibility. Neighbors who want to help are generally better served by giving money through an established fund than by dropping off clothing or household goods, which displaced families often have no place to store while they are in temporary housing.

title: Fort Worth Mariposa Park Apartment Fire Displaces About 50
description: A three-alarm fire at Mariposa Park Apartments in west Fort Worth damaged about 50 units and injured five people, including a firefighter, on Aug. 25.
key_points: A pre-dawn, three-alarm fire on Aug. 25 at Mariposa Park Apartments on Calmont Avenue damaged or destroyed roughly 50 apartments.
Five people were treated, including one firefighter, and reports put the number displaced at roughly 50 to 57 residents.
The Red Cross ran an evacuation center at the R.D. Evans Community Center, and the cause remains under investigation.
body_html:
Dozens of residents of a west Fort Worth apartment complex were forced from their homes before sunrise on Tuesday, Aug. 25, when a three-alarm fire tore through Mariposa Park Apartments on Calmont Avenue. Fire officials said about 50 apartments were damaged, and five people were treated for injuries, including one firefighter.

What happened

Fort Worth Fire Department crews were dispatched at about 5:30 a.m. to a reported apartment fire at the complex in the 6700 block of Calmont Avenue, near Interstate 30 and Green Oaks Boulevard, the department said on X. The department said crews arrived within two minutes, but the fire was already well advanced, and the response grew to three alarms.

According to Tech Times, the affected building is a two-story, wood-frame "garden" style structure with lightweight roof trusses and open attic space, which allowed fire to travel horizontally through the attic and reach the roofline before crews could stop it.

Who was affected

Roughly 50 apartments were destroyed or damaged. Early estimates that as many as 100 people were displaced were later revised; NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth reported about 50 people displaced, while other reports cited 57 residents.

Five people were treated: one firefighter, who was treated for smoke inhalation and returned to duty, and four civilians. Two of the civilians were taken to hospitals; their conditions were not released. One resident told NBC 5 that everything lost "can be replaced, in time."

The fire came less than a day after two Fort Worth firefighters were hospitalized with burns following a mayday at a wind-driven house fire on Crowley Road the night before, Tech Times reported. Both firefighters were rescued by a rapid intervention team.

Response and aid

The American Red Cross opened an evacuation center at the R.D. Evans Community Center, 3242 Lackland Road, and provided food, water, toiletries, pet supplies and teddy bears for children, according to NBC 5. Residents in need of help can call 1-800-RED-CROSS.

Cause and investigation

The cause has not been determined. Investigators said they were waiting for the structure to be declared safe to enter before beginning their work, and both the apartment fire and the previous night's house fire remain under investigation.

Why garden-style complexes burn fast, and what renters can do

Two- and three-story garden apartments are among the most common rental housing types in Texas and across the Sun Belt. Many older complexes lack sprinklers in attics, where a fire can run the length of a building before anyone below sees flames. That is why early warning and fast exits matter so much.

  • Treat any alarm as real. Leave immediately, knock on neighbors' doors if it is safe, and call 911 from outside.
  • Close doors behind you. A closed door slows the spread of smoke and fire to stairwells and neighboring units.
  • Check your smoke alarm. Texas law requires landlords to install smoke alarms and to inspect them at the start of a tenancy, and to repair or replace them when a tenant reports a problem. Make your request in writing.
  • Keep renters insurance current. Policies typically cover belongings and pay for hotels and meals if your unit is unlivable.
  • After a fire, ask about your lease. Texas law allows either party to end a lease when a unit is totally unusable because of fire damage not caused by the tenant, and may entitle you to a prorated rent refund. Ask management about your deposit and any prepaid rent, and get answers in writing.

Mariposa Park residents who still need assistance should contact the Red Cross North Texas region. Tenants elsewhere can use this fire as a prompt to photograph their belongings, store a copy of their lease online and confirm their renters policy is active.

title: Lightning Fire at Wesley Chapel Apartments Leaves 167 Displaced
description: A lightning strike set off a three-alarm fire at Cobalt Apartments in Wesley Chapel, Florida, destroying a building and displacing more than 160 residents.
key_points: Lightning struck Building 2 at Cobalt Apartments on Aug. 20, igniting an attic fire that destroyed the building; 167 residents in 83 apartments were displaced.
The strike disabled fire alarm panels, and the fire chief said the fire had a head start of about 25 minutes before anyone called 911.
Pasco County officials noted that lightning protection and attic sprinklers are not required for most apartment buildings under current rules.
body_html:
A single lightning strike during an afternoon storm destroyed an apartment building in Wesley Chapel, Florida, last month and displaced more than 160 residents. Weeks later, the fire at Cobalt Apartments has raised questions about how well older safety rules protect renters in buildings where a fire can start where no detector can see it.

What happened

Lightning struck the roof of Building 2 at Cobalt Apartments, 4434 Cobalt Brook Blvd., at about 2:26 p.m. on Thursday, Aug. 20, according to Pasco County Fire Rescue as reported by FOX 13 Tampa Bay. The fire grew to three alarms, and Tampa Fire Rescue and Hillsborough County Fire Rescue assisted Pasco crews, CBS12 reported. Firefighters worked through the night, and the fire was out roughly 12 hours later.

The strike knocked out the building's fire alarm panels, and the fire burned in the attic above the reach of most detection systems. Pasco County Fire Rescue Chief Ryan Guynn said the blaze burned for roughly 25 minutes before anyone called 911, telling FOX 13, "We were behind the ball from the start."

Who was affected

More than 90 units were evacuated on the day of the fire, and early estimates put the number displaced at about 200. A later update from FOX 13 put the final count at 167 residents from 83 apartments. No residents or firefighters were injured. Crews rescued dozens of pets, though six animals on the top floor were initially unaccounted for.

The building suffered multiple interior and roof collapses and was declared a total loss and condemned. FOX 13 reported that it was "highly unlikely" residents would be able to retrieve belongings before demolition, for which no start date had been announced.

Response and aid

The American Red Cross and Pasco County Emergency Management provided emergency shelter and connected residents to resources. According to FOX 13, 21 households were relocated within Cobalt, six moved to sister communities and the rest made their own arrangements. Residents also received donated necessities, gift cards, meals, veterinary services and help documenting insurance claims. The leasing office at 4338 Cobalt Brook Blvd. collected donations.

Management said it has offered relocation options, rent credits and deposit processing. An Orlando law firm said it represents more than two dozen displaced residents seeking compensation, FOX 13 reported.

Cause and code questions

Fire officials attributed the fire to the lightning strike. Lightning also damaged alarm systems in Buildings 1 and 3. Building 1's system was repaired and approved by the fire marshal, while Building 3 remained under repair with a continuous fire watch.

County officials said current codes do not require sprinklers in attics, and multifamily buildings under three stories did not require sprinkler systems at all until around 2020 to 2021. Lightning protection is not required for most buildings, and a 2018 proposal to the Florida Building Commission to mandate it was not adopted, officials said.

What renters should take from this

  • Ask what protects your building. Before signing a lease, ask whether the building has sprinklers, including in the attic, and when the alarm system was last inspected.
  • Do not rely on building alarms alone. Make sure your unit has working smoke alarms, and consider a battery-powered alarm that keeps working if a building system fails.
  • Get renters insurance. In a total loss, belongings and temporary housing costs fall on tenants who are not insured. Florida's storm season makes this coverage especially important.
  • Keep records off-site. Store copies of your lease, IDs and an inventory of belongings in the cloud so you can file claims even if you cannot re-enter.
  • Know your lease rights. Florida law lets tenants end a lease or reduce rent when a casualty that is not their fault makes a unit wholly or partly unlivable. Get any agreement with management in writing.

title: CO Leak at Gaithersburg Apartments Sends 12 to Hospitals
description: A faulty oven caused a carbon monoxide leak at Streamside Apartments in Gaithersburg, Maryland, sending 12 people, including seven children, to hospitals.
key_points: A carbon monoxide leak at Streamside Apartments on Sept. 5 led to more than 50 residents being evaluated and 12 taken to hospitals.
Washington Gas traced the carbon monoxide to an oven inside the building at 422 N. Summit Ave., and the oven was removed.
One child was sent to Baltimore Shock Trauma for possible hyperbaric treatment; residents were later allowed back into their homes.
body_html:
A carbon monoxide leak at a Gaithersburg, Maryland, apartment complex sent 12 people to hospitals on Saturday, Sept. 5, most of them children, after an oven filled two adjoining buildings with the colorless, odorless gas, fire officials said.

What happened

Montgomery County Fire and Rescue Service crews were called to Streamside Apartments at 422 N. Summit Ave. at about 8:45 a.m. on reports of a possible gas leak affecting several residents, according to FOX 5 DC. Crews found dangerously high carbon monoxide readings at 422 and elevated readings at the neighboring building at 420. Buildings 420, 422 and 424 were evacuated as a precaution.

Who was affected

More than 50 residents from the three buildings were evaluated by medics. Fire and rescue spokesperson David Pazos confirmed that 12 people were transported, four adults and seven children among them, The MoCo Show reported. One child, listed as stable, was sent to Baltimore Shock Trauma to be evaluated for hyperbaric treatment, which delivers high-pressure oxygen to clear carbon monoxide from the blood. Officials said all of the patients were expected to recover. Some early reports gave slightly lower hospital counts before officials confirmed the final figure.

Cause

Washington Gas responded and traced the gas to a faulty oven in the building at 422 N. Summit Ave. The oven was removed, and residents were allowed to return to their homes later that morning, with building management remaining on-site, according to The MoCo Show. Officials have not said what was wrong with the appliance.

Why carbon monoxide is a renter issue

Carbon monoxide is produced whenever fuel such as natural gas, propane or wood burns. A gas stove, furnace or water heater that is damaged, poorly vented or used improperly can release it into a home, and in apartment buildings it can seep into neighboring units through shared walls, ceilings and ductwork. Early symptoms such as headache, dizziness, nausea and fatigue are easy to mistake for the flu, and children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions face the greatest danger.

Many states and localities require carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances. Renters who are unsure what applies to their unit should ask their landlord and their local housing code office.

What tenants can do

  • Make sure you have a CO alarm. It should be on every sleeping level and near bedrooms. Test it monthly and replace it according to the manufacturer's date, often every five to seven years.
  • Never use a gas oven or stovetop to heat your home. Long, unvented use can raise carbon monoxide levels quickly.
  • Report problems in writing. A yellow or flickering burner flame, soot, a strong odor, or an appliance that keeps shutting off can signal a problem. Ask management to have it inspected and keep a copy of your request.
  • Act fast if an alarm sounds or you feel sick. Get everyone, including pets, outside into fresh air and call 911. Do not go back in until firefighters say it is safe.
  • Know who to call. If a landlord will not fix a gas appliance, contact your gas utility's emergency line and your county housing code office.

Because carbon monoxide travels between units, one neighbor's appliance can endanger an entire building, as the Streamside incident showed when three buildings were evacuated. If your alarm goes off, knock on nearby doors on your way out if it is safe to do so, and let firefighters know which units may still be occupied. A working alarm costs little compared with the cost of a missed warning, and many fire departments and utilities offer free or discounted alarms to residents who ask.

title: Federal Way Apartment Fire Displaces 40; Cooking Blamed
description: An unattended stovetop fire at a Federal Way, Washington, apartment complex spread to the third floor on Sept. 24, displacing about 40 residents from 18 units.
key_points: A fire at the Crestview West Apartments on Pacific Highway South displaced about 40 people from 18 units on Sept. 24.
Investigators said the fire was accidental, starting with cooking oil and French fries left unattended on a stovetop.
No one was injured, and the Red Cross opened a temporary shelter at the Federal Way Community Center.
body_html:
A kitchen fire that started with unattended cooking oil on a stovetop forced about 40 people from their homes at a Federal Way, Washington, apartment complex on Thursday afternoon, Sept. 24, investigators said. No one was hurt, but the fire spread from one unit to the floor above and left 18 apartments empty.

The fire is a reminder of how quickly a routine meal can turn into a building-wide emergency, and of how much neighbors in multifamily housing depend on one another's habits in the kitchen.

Timeline

The fire broke out in a single second-floor apartment at the Crestview West Apartments in the 27900 block of Pacific Highway South, according to KIRO 7. South King Fire crews found heavy smoke and flames coming from the unit and called a second alarm, KOMO News reported. The fire extended to the third floor before firefighters brought it under control.

Who was affected

The American Red Cross initially reported 25 people displaced, but revised the number upward to about 40 people from 18 units, according to FOX 13 Seattle. All occupants evacuated safely, and no injuries to residents or firefighters were reported.

Response and aid

Red Cross Disaster Action Team volunteers worked with displaced residents on shelter, food and clothing. A temporary shelter opened at the Federal Way Community Center, 876 S. 333rd St. The Red Cross encouraged evacuees to bring medication, clothing, blankets and comfort items for family members.

Cause

Investigators determined the fire was accidental. It began with cooking oil and French fries left unattended on a stovetop, KIRO 7 reported. The King County Sheriff's Office Fire Investigation Unit handled the investigation.

Why cooking fires matter for apartment dwellers

Cooking is the leading cause of home fires and home fire injuries in the United States, according to the National Fire Protection Association, and unattended cooking is the most common factor. In apartment buildings, one kitchen fire can displace dozens of neighbors, as it did here, because smoke, flames and the water used to fight them reach units above, below and beside the one where the fire began.

Stovetop safety basics

  • Stay in the kitchen when frying. If you need to leave, even briefly, turn off the burner.
  • Never use water on a grease fire. Slide a lid over the pan and turn off the heat. Water can make burning oil splatter and spread.
  • Keep a lid and an extinguisher handy. Ask your landlord whether a fire extinguisher is provided, and learn how to use it before you ever need it.
  • Keep the cooktop clear. Towels, paper, packaging and oven mitts left near burners can catch fire quickly.
  • If the fire grows, get out. Close the door behind you, pull the building alarm if there is one, and call 911 from outside.

If your unit is damaged by a neighbor's fire

  • Contact your renters insurer quickly. Your own policy typically covers your belongings and temporary living costs, regardless of where the fire started.
  • Talk to management about rent and timelines. Ask for written answers about repairs, prorated rent and your deposit, and contact a local tenant resource if you have questions about your rights under Washington law.
  • Use Red Cross help. The agency can provide emergency lodging, basic supplies and referrals for longer-term recovery.
  • Track your expenses. Keep receipts for hotels, meals, laundry and replacement essentials. Insurers generally reimburse additional living costs only with documentation.
  • Check on your deposit. If you decide not to return, ask management in writing how and when your security deposit and any prepaid rent will be handled.

Residents displaced by the Crestview West fire who still need help can contact the Red Cross Northwest Region or call 1-800-RED-CROSS.

title: South Huntsville Apartment Fire Destroys 16 Units
description: An early fire at a South Huntsville apartment complex on Meadowbrook Drive displaced residents of 16 units on Oct. 6, the area's second such fire in 10 days.
key_points: A fire early on Oct. 6 at an apartment complex on SW Meadowbrook Drive displaced residents of 16 apartments in building 19.
Police said no people or pets were hurt; the fire started in a middle unit and spread through the building, and the cause is under investigation.
It followed a Sept. 26 fire at Cambridge Court Apartments in South Huntsville that killed two dogs and sent one resident to the hospital.
body_html:
Residents of 16 apartments in South Huntsville, Alabama, are without homes after a fire ripped through an apartment building early Tuesday, Oct. 6. It was the second apartment fire in that part of the city in about 10 days.

What happened

Huntsville Fire and Rescue units were called shortly after 1 a.m. to an apartment complex on SW Meadowbrook Drive, just off Memorial Parkway, after several 911 callers reported flames coming from one of the buildings, according to WZDX/FOX54, which identified the complex as Indigo at Grissom. Video from the scene showed fire pushing through the roof, and WAFF reported multiple firefighters working near the complex.

The Huntsville Police Department told WHNT News 19 that the fire started in a middle unit of building 19 and spread through the entire building.

Who was affected

Huntsville Fire and Rescue District Chief Jay Gates said the residents of 16 apartments were displaced, WHNT reported, and the apartments were described as a complete loss. Police said no people or pets were injured. The total number of residents affected had not been released as of Tuesday morning.

Response and aid

The American Red Cross was on scene helping displaced residents. The agency typically provides emergency lodging, food, clothing and other basic needs, along with help planning next steps.

Cause

The cause had not been determined, and investigators remained on scene Tuesday morning. Officials had not said whether the building had sprinklers or whether smoke alarms sounded.

A second fire in 10 days

On Saturday night, Sept. 26, firefighters responded at about 8:15 p.m. to Cambridge Court Apartments, west of the Memorial Parkway and Lily Flagg intersection, WAFF reported. That fire stayed mostly in one apartment of a 12-unit building, and all residents got out, but two dogs died. Firefighters rescued four other dogs. One resident was taken to a hospital for smoke inhalation and was expected to recover. Huntsville Fire and Rescue Capt. Cory Green said crews were glad to have saved the other four dogs. The Red Cross also assisted residents, and the cause of that fire remains under investigation.

What renters can do now

When a fire starts in a middle unit and spreads through an entire building, residents of every apartment can lose their homes in minutes. For tenants in South Huntsville and anywhere else, a few steps can make a big difference:

  • Have a pet plan. Keep leashes and carriers near the door, and put a rescue sticker on a window so firefighters know animals may be inside. Never go back into a burning building for a pet; tell firefighters instead.
  • Test smoke alarms monthly. Press the test button, replace batteries as needed, and report missing or broken alarms to your landlord in writing so there is a record of the request.
  • Carry renters insurance. It can replace belongings and pay for a hotel while you look for a new place. Your landlord's policy does not cover your possessions.
  • If you are displaced, document everything. Photograph the damage when it is safe, keep receipts for emergency spending, and ask management in writing about prorated rent, your security deposit and whether you can transfer to another unit.
  • Replace documents early. Request replacement IDs, Social Security cards and benefit cards as soon as possible; the Red Cross can help with referrals.

Residents affected by the Meadowbrook Drive fire can contact the American Red Cross at 1-800-RED-CROSS. Neighbors in other buildings at the complex may also want to check that their own smoke alarms work and that hallways and stairwells are clear, since a fire in one building can quickly put nearby residents on alert.

title: Escondido Senior Apartment Fire Hospitalizes 5; Dogs Rescued
description: A second-floor fire at a senior apartment community in Escondido, California, sent five people to hospitals and temporarily displaced more than 30 residents.
key_points: A fire on Sept. 9 at a three-story senior apartment community at 1225 E. Grand Ave. in Escondido sent five people to hospitals.
Several residents were rescued from balconies, about a dozen dogs were saved, and more than 30 residents were displaced after power was cut.
The cause is under investigation; the Red Cross assisted displaced residents.
body_html:
Five people were taken to hospitals and about a dozen dogs were rescued after fire tore through two apartments at a senior living community in Escondido, California, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, city officials said.

What happened

The fire was reported at about 10:12 a.m. at a three-story apartment complex at 1225 E. Grand Ave., according to a City of Escondido news release. Fire officials requested a second alarm because of reports of trapped victims and the potential for the fire to spread. NBC 7 San Diego identified the property as Summerfield Villas, a senior apartment community, and reported that two second-story apartments were fully engulfed and several residents were rescued from balconies.

Firefighters kept the fire to the second floor, though multiple apartments sustained major damage. The response included 11 engines, two trucks, seven rescue ambulances, a light and air unit and three battalion chiefs, with help from San Marcos Fire, Valley Center Fire Protection District, Rancho Santa Fe Fire Protection District and San Diego Fire-Rescue. Escondido police, SDG&E, the San Diego Humane Society and the American Red Cross also responded.

Who was affected

Five people were taken to area hospitals, the city said. NBC 7 reported injuries including smoke inhalation and possible broken bones. Four police officers were evaluated for smoke inhalation and released, and no firefighters were hurt.

The city initially said an unknown number of residents had been displaced. NBC 7 reported that more than 30 residents were displaced after SDG&E shut off power to the entire building for several hours. Residents gathered in a community room after the evacuation, according to the Escondido Times-Advocate.

Animals rescued

Firefighters rescued about a dozen dogs and an unknown number of cats from adjoining apartments. From one unit, three adult dogs and eight puppies about 4 weeks old were passed through a window to firefighters below, the Times-Advocate reported. San Diego Humane Society veterinarians evaluated roughly two dozen animals for smoke inhalation, and none needed critical care. The dogs were taken to the society's Escondido campus for emergency boarding.

Cause

The cause of the fire is under investigation. SDG&E secured electrical and gas service to the building.

The power shutoff shows how a fire confined to two apartments can still affect an entire building. Residents whose units were untouched by flames still had to leave for hours because the utility needed to cut service, a disruption that can be especially hard for older adults who depend on powered medical equipment, refrigerated medications or elevators.

Fire safety for older renters and their families

Older adults face a higher risk of dying in home fires than the general population, according to the U.S. Fire Administration, in part because limited mobility, hearing loss or medications can slow an escape. Senior apartment residents and their families can prepare ahead:

  • Plan for mobility. If you use a walker or wheelchair, or cannot manage stairs quickly, tell building management and ask how evacuations work. Keep mobility aids, glasses and hearing aids within reach of the bed.
  • Use alarms you can hear or see. Strobe or bed-shaker smoke alarms are available for people with hearing loss. Ask your landlord about installing one as an accommodation.
  • Know your balcony. Keep balconies clear so firefighters can reach you if hallways are blocked by smoke.
  • Prepare for pets. Keep carriers and leashes close and a list of your animals on file with management.
  • Keep a go-bag. Include a list of medications, doctor contacts, copies of IDs and insurance cards.
  • Insure your belongings. Renters insurance can cover replacement costs and temporary housing if a fire or a power shutoff keeps you out of your unit.
